inline.s: [The knowing of emptiness and stillness] is also called the numinous knowing. [To realize that all marks are empty, the mind is naturally without thought; when a thought arises, immediately be aware of it, and being aware, it is gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies entirely in this.] To realize that all marks are illusory, the mind is naturally without thought (this is the dream-illusion contemplation spoken of earlier). If a deluded thought arises, you must at once realize that it is taking illusion as real and being turned by illusory marks. Realizing this, the deluded thought instantly vanishes (this requires the power of concentration to cut off delusion on the spot; the practice is precisely in this). The wondrous gate of practice is right here!
Realizing that all marks are empty, the mind is naturally without thought; when a thought arises, be aware of it, and being aware, it goes away.”
This is the very essence of concentration and wisdom in union!

blocks.text: 3. Not letting go of a single thought, passing through every thought

inline.s: In investigating [the huatou], what is prized is true practice and actual realization, in order to put an end to birth and death. Not letting go of a single thought — that is true practice; passing through every thought — that is actual realization. In daily activity, not apart from a single dharma, not settled in a single dharma, at every point not letting go, passing through each one — this is genuine effort.

[Not letting go] That is, not being deluded by it. [Passing through] That is, not being enveloped by it, not going along with its manipulations, not taking it as a real thing, and still less being held hostage by it.
Master Hanshan instructed:
Practitioners of recent times are ever farther from the sages and do not see the true practice-walk of the ancients,
(that is)

but in the realms manifest in daily use, at the brink of birth and death, pass through each and every one. This very daily use — not apart from a single dharma, not settled in a single dharma, at every point not lightly letting go — is genuine effort. Wherever in the present sounds and forms, favorable and adverse, loved and hated realms, you are able to pass through each one, that is the true gateway of awakening. And in this very awakening, head after head and dharma after dharma, is the real Buddha-dharma.

If you can, at the points in daily use where thoughts arise and stir, where the root of feeling is firmly knotted, where love and hate interlace and are hard to untie, where the habitual tendencies of greed, anger, delusion, and pride are hard to wear away — there, at the very root of the pain, plant an awl
(same as ‘pierce’)
and investigate each and every one to the bottom,
(as dream, illusion, bubble, shadow)
passing through each one,
(cutting off deluded thoughts)
this is true knowledge
(this is to be a true good and wise friend)
; and then at once you ascend to the unhindered, freely at ease, great liberation, the supreme dharma-gate. Apart from this, what other knowledge
(good and wise friend)
is there to consult
(to seek out)
? What more extraordinary dharma-gate is there to enter?”
(See the notes in
True Practice, Real Realization
the essay

In the study of concentration and wisdom in union, there is a very important lesson: seeing is just seeing, hearing is just hearing, being aware is just being aware, knowing is just knowing, without giving rise to thoughts. — Not grasping at marks, still and unmoved in Thusness.
According to the Theravada scripture, the Udana:

There was a practitioner named Bahiya, who after a long, dusty journey arrived at Savatthi to seek the Dharma from the Buddha. Just then he saw the Buddha going door to door in the city for alms, every movement graceful and sublime, with the six sense faculties fully tamed, guarded, and at peace. Bahiya drew near, bowed at his feet, and asked the Buddha to teach him the Dharma — to teach him the Dharma of immeasurable benefit and peace. The Buddha said that he was then going door to door for alms and it was not fitting to teach. But Bahiya pleaded repeatedly, and so the Buddha taught him on the spot:

“Bahiya! You should train thus: in seeing, only what is seen; in hearing, only what is heard; in knowing, only what is known; in being aware, only what is aware. Bahiya! When you can be such that in seeing only the seen, in hearing only the heard, in knowing only the known, in being aware only the aware, then you will have reached freedom from attachment and obstruction. If you are free from attachment and obstruction, then you have no past life and no future life. You have not these two lives of past and future
(but only the present)
; all sorrow, lamentation, distress, and suffering will thereby be dispersed and vanish.”

[The three times] The past, present, and future. Whatever has arisen and ceased is called the ‘past’; whatever has arisen and not yet ceased is called the ‘present’; whatever has not been born and not yet arisen is called the ‘future’. [But only the present] The scripture says:
“In seeing, only the seen; in hearing, only the heard; in knowing, only the known; in being aware, only the aware.”
and without deluded thoughts about past or future. Indeed, the unease, anxiety, and suffering in people’s minds all arise from deluded imaginings about the past or the future.

blocks.text: 4. Dissolving karma, eradicating offenses, and bestowing blessings

inline.s: The Sutra of the Contemplation of the Practice of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva says:
“The ocean of all karmic hindrances is born of deluded thought. If you wish to repent, sit upright and contemplate reality. All offenses are like frost and dew — the sun of wisdom can dispel them.”
ocean of karmic hindrances
Karmic hindrances as deep and vast as the great sea.
all offenses like frost and dew, the sun of wisdom can dispel them
Just as the sun melts away frost and dew, contemplating reality (the sun of wisdom) can dispel all offenses.
As for “
contemplating reality
”, Master Hanshan explained
“A mind with no things is called reality.”
see
Essentials of Chan and Pure Land
, the chapter ‘The Sun of Wisdom Dispels Offenses’)

The mind that is without thought is a mind without things; sitting upright without thought is like the sun melting snow, frost, and dew — dissolving karma and eradicating offenses. This is repentance through reality:

“Offenses arise from the mind, so repent with the mind; when the mind is gone, offenses too are extinguished. When both the mind and its offenses are gone, both are empty — this is called true repentance.”
In the chapter ‘The Sun of Wisdom Dispels Offenses’, Master Hanshan instructed:

[Now, being in the dream of ignorance, how can one dissolve past karma? One must use the light of wisdom to break through ignorance, and be certain that one’s own mind is originally pure, not driven by deluded, inverted thought; then all karma has no cause, for deluded thought is the cause of all karma. Why is this? Because from beginningless time one has been deluded about one’s own mind, and life after life, with a deluded mind, created all sorts of karma. These karmic habits accumulate within the field of the eight consciousnesses, watered by the water of ignorance, so that this evil seed sprouts karmic shoots. This is the root of offense, and all evil karma arises from it.]

So now, being in the dream of ignorance, how can one dissolve past karma? One must use the light of wisdom to break through ignorance, be certain that one’s own mind is originally pure, and not be driven by deluded, inverted thought. Then there is no cause for creating karma, for deluded thought is the cause of all karma. Why is this? Because from beginningless kalpas one has been deluded about one’s own mind, and life after life, with a deluded mind, created all sorts of karma. These karmic habits accumulate in the alaya-vijnana (the eighth consciousness), watered by the water of ignorance, so that this evil seed sprouts karmic shoots. This is the root of offense, and all evil karma arises from it.
[Now, to dissolve past karma, you must first rouse the great light of wisdom to break through ignorance, not allowing deluded thoughts to sprout and grow in secret.
If you can, at the very point where a deluded thought arises, cut it off with a single thought, then the accumulated root of past karma is dissolved on the spot.

As the saying goes, do not fear the arising of thoughts, only fear that awareness is too slow. If awareness comes a little too late, then one is turned by them. If you can, at the points in daily use where thoughts arise and stir, be aware thought after thought and extinguish thought after thought, this is what is meant by ‘all offenses are like frost and dew — the sun of wisdom can dispel them’. Since the darkness of ignorance can be broken only by wisdom, this is what is meant by wisdom being able to dispel them.]
Now, to dissolve past karma, you must first rouse the great light of wisdom to break through ignorance, not allowing deluded thoughts to sprout and grow in secret.
If you can, at the very point where a deluded thought arises, cut it off with a single thought, then the root of karma accumulated in the past is dissolved on the spot.

As the saying goes, ‘do not fear the arising of thoughts, only fear that awareness is too slow’. If awareness comes a little too late, then one is turned by it (deluded thought). If you can, at the points in everyday life where thoughts arise and stir, be aware thought after thought and extinguish thought after thought, this is ‘all offenses are like frost and dew — the sun of wisdom can dispel them’. Since the darkness of ignorance can be broken only by wisdom, this is how wisdom is able to dispel all offenses.

[If, day and night without ceasing, you diligently observe and do not let it pass, then right at the place where deluded thought arises, you investigate to the very bottom the mark of non-arising. Looking again and again, in the end it is unobtainable. After a long time it becomes familiar and mature, and your own mind is pure and without things; a mind without things is reality. If you constantly contemplate this mind, what deluded thought could be accommodated, what accumulated karma could find lodging? This way of using the mind is called the samadhi of contemplation-and-observation.]

You must, day and night without ceasing, diligently observe and not let it pass, but right at the place where deluded thought arises, investigate to the very bottom the mark of non-arising. Looking again and again, the deluded thought is in the end unobtainable. After a long time it becomes familiar and mature, and your own mind is pure and without things,
a mind without things is reality

. If you constantly contemplate this pure mind, what deluded thought could be accommodated, what accumulated karma could find lodging? This way of using the mind is called the samadhi of contemplation-and-observation.

[If, day and night without ceasing, diligently observe] Here ‘ruo’ means ‘you’. For example: ‘If we change your service and restore your levy, then what do you say?’ (This line is from Liu Zongyuan’s ‘The Snake-Catcher’; rendered as: ‘Change your task of catching snakes and restore your tax levy — how would you find that?’)
Master Hanshan further instructed:
“Therefore the Buddha-dharma teaches people, first of all, to
(exclusively to)
make the severing of deluded thought the foundation,
(because)

deluded thought is the root of all manner of evil karma such as greed, anger, and delusion. Even the bodhisattva’s practice leading to Buddhahood, reaping the most sublime, adorned, and vast field of blessings in heaven and among humans, all begins with severing deluded thought.
As
(because)
deluded thought being severed, evil karma is dissolved; evil karma being dissolved, a hundred blessings gather. This is what is meant by seeking abundant blessings for oneself.
(from the Collected Works of a Dream-Wanderer
for Zhong Hengying)

blocks.text: 4. Both subject and object extinguished (seeing the original nature)

inline.s: Alone the numinous light shines, wholly freed from faculties and dust.

The extinguishing of both subject and object: the mind that observes (investigates) and the realm that is observed (investigated) are together extinguished, and the body, mind, and world at once fade away, while the ten quarters shine all round and bright. This is the state of having thoroughly seen one’s original nature; the Chan school calls it seeing the mind and realizing the nature. For the Pure Land school, this is the attainment of the Buddha-recitation samadhi.
(See
Master Yinguang’s
Groping the Elephant of the Buddha-Recitation Samadhi

[Original nature] The original nature is also called Buddha-nature, the original face, or thusness. Because the original nature is Buddha, it is named Buddha-nature; because the original nature is the primordial state of self-nature, it is named the original face, also abbreviated as the original; because the original nature is unchanging and constant, it is named thusness. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“The original nature is Buddha; apart from that nature there is no other Buddha.”
For more on the original nature, see
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathagatagarbha
the essay.
Chan Master Baizhang, entering the hall, said:

“Alone the numinous light shines, wholly freed from faculties and dust. The essence is revealed as true and constant, not bound by words and letters. The mind-nature is undefiled, of itself wholly perfected. Only leave the conditions of delusion, and you are the Buddha of Thusness.”
(from the Compendium of the Five Lamps)

[Wholly freed from faculties and dust] The six sense faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) and the six sense objects (form, sound, scent, taste, touch, and dharma) are utterly separated. [Conditions of delusion] To cling on one’s own deludedly; here ‘condition’ is a verb. [Only leave the conditions of delusion and you are the Buddha of Thusness] As long as you are free of deluded self-clinging, you are the dharmakaya Buddha. The Lankavatara Sutra says:
: ‘the Dharma Buddha
(dharmakaya Buddha)
is free from clinging.’
The Diamond Sutra says:
“Free from all marks, this is called being a Buddha.”
[Buddha of Thusness] The Buddha who is awakened to the principle-substance of Thusness, that is, the dharmakaya Buddha. The Lankavatara Sutra says:
“What is the nirmita Buddha? What is the sambhoga Buddha? What is the Buddha of Thusness?”
Master Hanshan said:
“Watch
(investigate)
until you reach the point where a single thought does not arise; then the boundaries of before and after are broken, and the middle stands alone. Suddenly the lacquer bucket is smashed,
and you at once see the original face.
Then body, mind, and the world at once sink away
(same as ‘sink’)
, like the shadows of sky-flowers falling
(the illusory shadows of sky-flowers cease)

; the ten quarters shine all round and bright, forming one great treasury of light. Only then is it the time of arriving home; in daily use it is present before you, bright and perfectly clear, beyond all doubt. Only then do you trust that your own mind is of itself thus. The buddhas and patriarchs of old, in their own personal enjoyment, are no different and no other.”
the Collected Works of a Dream-Wanderer
on the Essentials of Buddha-Recitation and Chan Investigation
Master Hanshan again said:
“Only within thought after thought,
watch and investigate where thought has not yet arisen.
Because of thus abiding apart from thought, after a long time
(only the single thought of watching and investigating remains)
, suddenly the thought
(the single thought of watching and investigating)
breaks asunder, and mind and realm are both forgotten
(the character is used in the sense of ‘extinguished’)
; like a lion freed from its leash, roaming at ease.”
(from the Collected Works of a Dream-Wanderer, instructing the Chan practitioner Liaoxin Hai)

[Mind and realm both forgotten (the character is used in the sense of ‘extinguished’)] The mind and realm are both extinguished. This is the state of the extinguishing of both subject and object: the mind that watches and investigates and the realm that is watched and investigated are together extinguished, which is also the state of seeing the mind and realizing the nature.
“The great Way is vast and open, utterly free of thought and reflection.”

The whole process of Chan contemplation is the process of stilling thought. When coarse thoughts are stilled, the ten thousand thoughts return to one; when fine thoughts are stilled, the one returns to nothing (as Elder Xuyun speaks of below as ‘the ten thousand thoughts suddenly stilled’); when the subtlest thoughts are briefly stilled, one sees the mind and realizes the nature.
[The great Way is vast and open, utterly free of thought and reflection] See
The Fourth Patriarch’s Instructions to Farong
the essay. [Coarse thought, fine thought, and subtlest thought]

Mental thoughts are of three kinds: coarse, fine, and subtlest. For example, for a practitioner of Buddha-recitation, a deluded thought is a coarse thought, and the thought of reciting the Buddha is a fine thought. Normally, when both coarse and fine thoughts are stilled, that is called no-thought (wunian) — this is what is usually meant by no-thought. Further, if the subtlest thoughts also cease, this is the ultimate no-thought. Therefore the meaning of the term ‘no-thought’ must be determined from context. For example,
the ‘no-thought’ in ‘the original mind is without thought’ refers to the ultimate no-thought.

[Subtlest thought] The subtle arising, ceasing, and flowing onward of the consciousness-mind, which is the mark of the alaya-vijnana. When the subtlest thoughts are briefly stilled, one sees the mind and realizes the nature; when the subtlest thoughts are forever stilled,
only the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment shines alone and remains
, then one fully realizes the fruit of Buddhahood. The Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana says:
“When a bodhisattva reaches the end of the grounds
(having fully cultivated the ten grounds)
and perfects the expedient means, then in one instant the awakening-mind first arises and yet the mind has no initial mark;
and because it is far from the subtlest thoughts,
it sees the mind-nature
; the mind is then abiding and constant,
and this is called ultimate awakening.
Master Guifeng said:
If the subtle flowing stream
(the subtlest thoughts)

is wholly stilled and extinguished, and only the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment shines alone and remains, then answering to conditions it manifests hundreds of thousands of millions of bodies to save sentient beings of karmic affinity,
and this is called being a Buddha.
(see the Record of the Transmission of the Lamp of the Jingde Era)
In the chronological biography of the Venerable Xuyun, Elder Xuyun recounts his awakening at the age of fifty-six:
The duties within the meditation hall did not assign me
(me)
to watch in turn, so I had the opportunity to practice. From then on
the ten thousand thoughts suddenly stilled
, the effort ‘settled onto the floor,’ day and night as one, and my movements were as swift as flying.

[Settled onto the floor] ‘Settled onto the floor’ means being real and substantial. Elder Xuyun said: ‘Only in Buddha-recitation must you gather the mind to contemplate and observe, every phrase settling onto the floor. To settle onto the floor means being real and substantial. Every phrase real, every thought in accord, and after a long time it naturally becomes one piece.’ (From Fragments of Instruction by Elder Xuyun)

One evening, during the night incense period, I opened my eyes and looked and suddenly saw a great light as bright as day, clear through within and without. Across the wall I saw the incense-lamp master relieving himself, and I saw the West-single master in the latrine
(qing, the latrine)

; and far off, boats moving on the river, and the trees on both banks in all their many colors — all of these I saw clearly. Only then did the three board-strikes sound. The next day I asked the incense-lamp and West-single masters, and indeed it was so. I knew this was a state [of insight] and did not find it strange.
By the eighth retreat of the twelfth month
(the eighth Chan retreat)

, on the third night, when the six-incense period was released from stillness, the attendant of the retreat as usual poured boiling water and it splashed upon my hand, and the teacup fell to the ground. With the sound of breaking, the root of doubt was suddenly cut off, filling my whole life with joy, as if waking from a dream. I thought to myself that in the decades I had wandered since leaving home, at the reed hut by the Yellow River, a common fellow once asked me a question, and I did not know what water was. If at that time I had kicked over the stove
(for what water was there!)
, what would Wen Ji have had to say? Had I not fallen into the water and fallen gravely ill, had I not met the guidance by favorable and adverse means, the good-and-wise friend’s
(good and wise friend)
instruction, I might have missed my whole life; how would there be
(how)
today? Therefore I composed this verse:
The cup falls and strikes the ground; the sound rings out crisp and clear;
Empty space itself is shattered, and the wild mind is at once stilled.
Another verse:
Scalding the hand, smashing the cup; home destroyed, people gone, words hard to speak;
Spring arrives, the fragrance of flowers blooms everywhere; the mountains, rivers, and great earth are the Tathagata.
Preserve: cut off thought and reflection.
Let be: let the mind be at ease and free.
When there is a matter that accords with principle, seeing it, do it; having done it, let it go;
done — what is there not done?

[A matter that accords with principle] Yi means principle and reason. In whatever one undertakes, one should first carefully examine right and wrong and benefit and harm; only when it accords with principle should one then act. This is the mind of waking-awareness, which is different from the mind of wildness and confusion. (See
Karma Cannot Bind

Preserving-and-letting-be (baoren) means preserving and then allowing spontaneous function — these are the two stages of purifying habitual tendencies after seeing the nature. ‘Preserving’ means doing one’s utmost to tend the sage-embryo so that it is not harmed by greed, anger, and delusion, in order to accomplish the first two of the four forbearances (the forbearance of suppression and the forbearance of gentle compliance); ‘letting be’ means that, once the sage-embryo has grown to maturity, following the circumstances and conditions it functions naturally, and is still further refined amid both favorable and adverse conditions, in order to accomplish the latter two of the four forbearances (the forbearance of non-arising and the forbearance of still extinction).

[The four forbearances] The forbearance of suppression, the forbearance of gentle compliance, the forbearance of non-arising, and the forbearance of still extinction. The forbearance of suppression: a beginning practitioner, desiring to endure both favorable and adverse circumstances (without giving rise to greed, anger, or delusion), must first subdue and tame the mind. The forbearance of gentle compliance: having tamed the mind for a long time, when encountering circumstances and conditions, one can endure naturally without forced restraint (without giving rise to greed, anger, or delusion); at this time the mind is gentle, soft, and compliant. The forbearance of non-arising: a person of the sage stage realizes that all dharmas are of themselves unarisen; both sentient and insentient things are dependently arisen and without self-nature, empty in their very substance; therefore, in this self-naturelessness, the forbearing mind does not move, and one personally realizes non-arising. The forbearance of still extinction: a sage at the fruit stage who thoroughly realizes the nirvana state of still extinction, where both the mark of movement and the mark of stillness accord with Thusness. [Thusness] The state of self-nature free of inverted discrimination. Because it is the thusness (the true mark of all dharmas) realized by the wisdom that accords with principle, it is called ‘Thusness’.

For one who has been pointed directly to see the nature (found the master of the house), one must first ‘preserve’ and then ‘let be’ — this is what is commonly called sudden awakening with gradual cultivation.

[Direct pointing to seeing the nature] As when Damei asked Mazu, ‘What is the Buddha?’ Mazu replied, ‘This very mind is the Buddha!’ Damei awakened greatly at these words (catching a glimpse of self-nature and finding the master of the house). Again, as when Lingxun asked Master Guizong, ‘What is the Buddha?’ Guizong said, ‘If I tell you now, I fear you will not believe it!’ Lingxun said, ‘The master speaks sincerely; how would I dare not believe!’ Guizong said, ‘You yourself are he!’ Lingxun had an insight at these words (catching a glimpse of self-nature and finding the master of the house).

For one who has passed through the ten thousand thoughts returning to one, and the one returning to nothing, and thus seen the mind and realized the nature (thoroughly seeing one’s original nature), this is what is commonly called gradual cultivation with sudden awakening. Since the effort of ‘preserving’ (cutting off thought and reflection — which the Chan community calls ‘the great death’) is already accomplished, one may then devote oneself to the effort of ‘letting be’ (letting the mind be at ease — which the Chan community calls ‘the great life’).
As for how to preserve and let be,
please read
Preserving and Letting Be Along with Conditions
and
The Fourth Patriarch’s Instructions to Farong
these two essays.
Question: What is the Buddha-recitation effort forming into a single piece?
Answer: When reciting the Buddha, do not intermingle deluded thoughts — the thought of reciting continues without interruption to form a single piece. Master Yinguang said:
“If the Buddha-recitation cannot be pure and single, you must restrain the mind so that it does not run outward; after a long time it will of itself become pure and single.
To form into a piece means being pure and without admixture.
(from the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang,
in the fourth letter to the layman Ma Qixi) Master Hanshan said:
“You must take this single sound of the Buddha
(the Buddha-name)
and hold it fast between your teeth,
and be certain to overcome deluded thought.

In every place, thought after thought, it is present before you, not shrouded by deluded thought. Practicing with such bitter, earnest effort, after a long time it becomes familiar and mature, and it naturally responds — without seeking to form into a piece, it forms into a piece of itself.”
(from the Collected Works of a Dream-Wanderer,
instructing the layman Jingxin)
Question: What is ‘beating into a single piece’?
Answer:
Master Hanshan instructed:

“If you can truly use the mind, exert effort solely before a single thought arises. After a long time it becomes familiar and mature, and with no thought arising, the original substance manifests before you. The constant light is bright and clear, unshaken in brightness and darkness, one and the same in motion and stillness; only then is it ‘beaten into a single piece’.”
(from the Collected Works of a Dream-Wanderer,
in answer to the monk Haiyin of Huzhou)
Question: When I am investigating the Buddha-recitation, my deluded thoughts have become far fewer, but when sluggishness strikes I am at a loss. How should I counter sluggishness?

Answer: When sluggishness strikes, you may pause your investigation to counter the sluggishness. The method is: rouse your spirit, at all times raise your head and gaze upward, and do abdominal deep breathing — inhale deeply through the nose (the abdomen protruding) and hold the breath
second, then exhale slowly (the abdomen contracting) and hold the breath
second, keeping each inhale-and-exhale at about

seconds. At the same time, recite the Buddha (on the in-breath recite ‘A-mi’, on the out-breath recite ‘tuo-fo’), and clearly be aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen. In this way, the sluggishness will gradually recede. When the sluggishness has gone, return to investigating the Buddha-recitation. You may also adopt the method taught by the ancient worthy in the Chan Pass Policy (compiled by Master Lianchi):
Brothers, having dozed so long on the meditation cushion
(having long sunk into sluggishness)

, you must get down and walk about a while, wash and rinse your mouth with cold water, open your eyes afresh, and then return to the cushion. Straighten up your spine, stand like a cliff of ten thousand fathoms, and lift the huatou single-mindedly.”
In recent times, few are those resolutely devoted to Chan contemplation. No sooner do they investigate a huatou than they are bound by the two demons of sluggishness
(sluggishness)
and scatteredness
(distraction)
; they do not know that sluggishness and distraction are precisely counteracted by the feeling of doubt
(not knowing that the feeling of doubt is precisely the sharp weapon against sluggishness and distraction)
. When faith is strong, the feeling of doubt must be strong; when the feeling of doubt is strong, sluggishness and distraction of themselves vanish.”
One day, in the corridor I met Xiu
(Venerable Xiu)
and was able to draw near to him.
Thereupon I asked: ‘Right now I cannot drive away sluggishness and distraction
(I cannot now get rid of sluggishness and distraction; what shall I do)

.’ Xiu said: ‘You are simply not fierce enough! You must sit high on the cushion, straighten up your spine, and gather your whole body into a single huatou — then what sluggishness or distraction are you still looking for
(where would there still be any sluggishness or distraction)
?’ Following Xiu, I practiced
(so I practiced according to Venerable Xiu’s words)
, and before I knew it both body and mind were forgotten. Clear and pure for three days and nights, my eyes never once closed.”
Throughout the twelve hours, utterly without a thing to cling to
(without the slightest attachment)
, contemplate the one before father and mother were born, which
(which)
one is my original face? Whether it takes effect or not, whether there is sluggishness and distraction or not, just keep lifting it up.”

If there are sluggishness and distraction, do not stir up thoughts to dispel them, but promptly lift up the huatou, rousing body and mind and summoning full vigor. If that does not work, get down and walk in mindful pacing; when you feel the sluggishness and distraction have gone, return to the cushion. Suddenly, without lifting it lifts itself, without doubting it doubts itself. Walking, you do not know you are walking; sitting, you do not know you are sitting. There is only the feeling of investigating, solitary and far-reaching, vivid and clear. This is called the place where afflictions are cut off, and likewise the place where the self is forgotten.”
Question: If the huatou is the word ‘wu’ (no), how should one investigate it?
Answer: If investigating the word ‘wu’, then look inward and investigate: Who is this one who lifts up the word ‘wu’?
Master Hanshan said:

“Single-mindedly raise a single gong-an (public case) as a huatou, such as ‘Zhaozhou: does a dog also have Buddha-nature or not? Zhaozhou said: No (wu)’, or ‘all dharmas return to one; where does the one return?’, or investigate ‘who is the one reciting the Buddha?’ Whatever one you raise, hold it laid across in your breast like the kingly vajra sword, cutting off in a single stroke all thoughts and deluded imaginings, as one cuts a tangled skein of silk. Within, do not let it out; without, do not let it in. Seal off the vital ford, plug up the throat, and do not allow a breath to escape. Exerting yourself thus,
with a single glance, look: what, in the end, is this one who lifts the huatou?
(from the Collected Works of a Dream-Wanderer, instructing the mountain master Songpu En)

Question: When I raise a single Buddha-name, I look inward to investigate who is reciting the Buddha. In this way, deluded thoughts become fewer and fewer, and the effort gradually gathers strength. My question is: after investigating this way for a long time, my head grows dizzy; or sometimes I find the practice hard, and if I grit my teeth and keep going, I also grow dizzy. What should I do?

Answer: This shows that your power of awareness is not yet strong enough. You can solve your problem this way: whenever you meet with trouble, such as dizziness and so on, go practice the preliminary practices (
the ‘Preliminary Practices’

chapter). Once you can do it smoothly, then return to your investigation. Persisting in this back-and-forth, the investigating effort will grow more and more powerful, and you will not grow dizzy. At the same time, remember the practical advice on practice: do not rush, and do not stop. Remind yourself of this at all times.
